Vegan Potato Crust Quiche (Gluten-Free)

by Sarah CobachoPublished: October 12, 2026

Jump to recipe

Add as a preferred source on Google

Instaread
A vegan potato crust quiche with mushroom, leek and spinach, set with blended mung beans. 21 g of protein a slice, and great for meal prep.
gluten-freehigh-fiberiron-richlower-calorienut-freesoy-free
vegan·high-fiber·iron-rich·lower-calorieGFgluten-freeView all →NFnut-freeView all →SFsoy-freeView all →

This delicious Vegan Potato Quiche with potato crust was actually an Instagram follower request! I just love it when you guys tell me what you’d like to see next. You always come up with the best ideas, so don’t hesitate to send me some requests in the comments.

Potato crust has been all over our feed lately, and I have a couple of delicious versions with cold fillings if you’d like to check them out, but this warm version might be my favorite one yet. We have a crispy mashed potato crust, which might be the best way to make a gluten-free crust. And the filling is so delicious, think caramelized leeks, mushrooms, and greens, all wrapped up in a high-protein filling.

Quiche filling is usually made with a mix of eggs and heavy cream, which can be quite high in saturated fat, so of course I had to give it a heart-healthy glow-up! I made my filling using mung beans. I got the idea from seeing JUST Egg, the egg replacement product, being rolled out around the world. Unfortunately, we don’t have it in Australia, but the good news is that you can make it at homemade for a budget-friendly and healthy option. It’s packed with protein, fiber (and this is where the advantage of plant protein really shows up), and some key micronutrients, including folate, magnesium, and iron. It works so well, is super quick to put together, and makes the most delicious high-protein filling for these quiches.

And now the best part: this is a great meal prep-friendly meal. Actually, as I type this, I have a slice in the air fryer because it’s a busy day and I don’t have time to make a full 30-minute lunch! You can have it for breakfast or for lunch with a delicious side of greens or a side salad. Each slice brings 21 g of protein, 14 g of fiber, and 6 mg of iron. French and nutritionist-approved!

Why I love this recipe (as a nutritionist)

  • Heart-healthy: a quiche normally gets its richness from butter pastry, cream and eggs. No saturated fat in this one, and in fact mung beans support heart health by lowering LDL (bad) cholesterol, reducing blood pressure, and improving blood vessel function.
  • Mung beans do the work of the eggs: soaked overnight and blended with soy milk, they set firm in the oven and carry the biggest share of the 21 g of protein in a slice. They’re the same bean the bottled vegan eggs are built from.
  • 14 g of fiber a slice: most of that is the potatoes and the mung beans. The potatoes also boil and then cool right down before you mash them into the pan, and cooling cooked potato forms resistant starch, which is great for your gut microbes.
  • Kala namak: a sulfurous black salt, it gives it an eggy taste, which is quite surprising.
  • 6 mg of iron: paired with allium to enhance absorption. Soaking the mung beans also make some of the nutrients easier to absorb.
  • Six slices out of one pan: it’s amazing for meal prep. I make it once, and breakfast or lunch is sorted for the rest of the week.

Ingredient notes

  • Potatoes: 3 lb sounds like a lot until you remember they’re the entire crust. They go into the pot whole and skin-on (for more fiber and iron!).
  • Dried split mung beans: these are the eggs. They soak for 4 hours or overnight, then blend with the soy milk into a batter that sets in the oven. There’s no swap for them here.
  • Kala namak: also sold as black salt or Himalayan black salt. It smells strongly of sulfur in the jar and that’s exactly the point, it reads as egg once it’s baked in.
  • Button mushrooms and leek: the mushrooms start in a dry pan so they give up their water first, and the leek goes in after and cooks down until it starts to caramelize.

Step by Step Photos

Press the cooled potatoes into an oiled springform pan with the bottom of a clean mug, working them evenly over the base and up the sides. Brush the surface generously with olive oil and bake at 425°F (220°C) for 25 minutes.

Start the sliced mushrooms in a large covered pan over medium heat with no oil, for 5 minutes, until they begin to release their liquid. Then add the olive oil, leek, garlic, sea salt flakes and dried thyme, and cook for about 10 minutes, until the leek starts to caramelize.

Stir in the baby spinach and cook until it just wilts, then set the pan aside. When the crust comes out of the oven, spread the filling straight over it.

Pour the blended mung bean mix over the top. It comes out of the blender bright yellow from the turmeric, smelling like eggs from the kala namak. Stir very gently, only enough to combine.

Bake at 400°F (205°C) for 25 minutes, then let it sit for 10 minutes before you release the springform ring. Slice it, and look at that layer of potato underneath! View recipe card below for detailed instructions.

Variations and tips

  • No kala namak: the ingredient list has the swap, sea salt flakes instead. It’s still delicious without!
  • Change what’s in the middle: mushroom, leek and spinach is the version I make, but the potato crust and the mung bean mix will take most vegetables you have in the drawer.
  • Conventional oven: the recipe is written for fan-forced. Without a fan, go about 35°F (20°C) hotter and turn the pan halfway through each bake.
  • What I serve it with: a simple side of greens. I love arugula with this, dressed with equal parts olive oil, Dijon mustard and balsamic vinegar.

FAQ

Is this potato crust quiche really gluten-free?+
Yes. There’s no pastry and no wheat flour anywhere in it, and the tapioca flour that binds the filling is naturally gluten-free. The only label worth a glance is the Dijon mustard, since a few brands use a wheat-based additive.
Can I make it nut-free?+
It already is. There are no nuts or peanuts in the crust, the filling or the mung bean mix.
Can I make it soy-free?+
The soy milk is the only soy in the recipe, so use another unsweetened plant milk in its place. Pick one with no added sugar or vanilla, because the mix is savory.
Do I really have to soak the mung beans?+
Yes. They soak for 4 hours or overnight in the refrigerator, then you drain and rinse them before they go in the blender. It’s the one part of this recipe you can’t start and finish in the same hour. It’s important for the texture, and it helps make some of the nutrients more absorbable.
How do I store the leftovers?+
Let the quiche cool, then keep it covered in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Reheat slices in the oven, or airfryer so the potato crust firms back up. It keeps in the fridge for 5 days, I do not recommend freezing.

Vegan Potato Crust Quiche (Gluten-Free)

Pinterest Facebook Share on XCopy link
Share SaveSaved! Comment
A quiche with a crust made entirely of potatoes, no pastry and no eggs. The filling is mushroom, leek and spinach, set with a blended mung bean mix, and one slice carries 21 g of protein.
Prep 20 minutes mins
Cook 1 hour hr 15 minutes mins
Soaking Time 4 hours hrs
Total 1 hour hr 35 minutes mins

Equipment

  • Springform Cake Pan
  • Blender
Servings –+

Ingredients

Potato Crust

  • 3 lb (1.4 kg) potatoes
  • 1 tbsp (15 ml) olive oil

Filling

  • 10 1/2 oz (300 g) button mushrooms - finely sliced
  • 1 leek - white and light green parts only, halved lengthwise and thinly sliced into half-moons
  • 1 tbsp (15 ml) olive oil
  • 5 garlic cloves - peeled and minced
  • 1/2 tsp (3 g) sea salt flakes
  • 1 tsp dried thyme
  • 3 cups (90 g) baby spinach

Mung Bean Egg Mix

  • 1 cup (200 g) dried split mung beans
  • 1 1/4 cups (300 ml) soy milk
  • 1/2 tsp (1 g) ground turmeric
  • 1/2 tsp (1 g) ground black pepper
  • 1/3 cup (40 g) nutritional yeast
  • 1 tbsp (8 g) tapioca flour
  • 1 tsp (4 g) kala namak - or swap for 1/2 of sea salt flakes – see notes
  • 1 tbsp Dijon mustard

Instructions

  • Soak the mung beans: Place the mung beans in a fine-mesh sieve and rinse thoroughly. Transfer to a large bowl, cover generously with water, and soak for 4 hours or overnight in the refrigerator. Drain and rinse thoroughly.
  • Prepare the potatoes: Add the potatoes to a large pot of cold salted water. Bring to a gentle boil and cook for about 25 minutes, until tender when pierced with a fork. Drain and allow to cool down.
  • Preheat the oven to 430°F (220°C), convection/fan on.
  • Shape and bake the potato crust: Lightly brush a 10-inch (25 cm) springform cake pan with olive oil. Place the cooled potatoes in the pan. Using the bottom of a clean mug, mash and press them evenly over the base and up the sides. Generously brush the surface with olive oil. Place the pan on the middle rack of the oven and bake for 25 minutes.
  • Prepare the filling: Add the sliced mushrooms to a large pan over medium heat. Cover and cook for 5 minutes, until they begin to release their liquid. Add the olive oil, leek, garlic, sea salt flakes, and dried thyme. Cook for about 10 minutes, until the leek starts to caramelize. Stir in the baby spinach and cook until just wilted. Set aside.
  • Prepare the mung bean egg mix: Add the soaked mung beans to a high-speed blender along with the soy milk, ground turmeric, ground black pepper, nutritional yeast, tapioca flour, and kala namak. Blend until perfectly smooth.
  • Assemble and bake: Remove the potato crust from the oven and reduce the temperature to 400°F (200°C), convection / fan on. Spread the filling and mung bean mix evenly over the crust, then stir very gently to combine. Return the springform pan to the middle rack and bake for 25 minutes. Remove from the oven and allow to cool for 10 minutes, then carefully release the springform ring, slice, and enjoy.

Notes

Fan-forced / convection vs conventional ovens: Fan-forced, also called convection, uses a fan to circulate hot air, so it cooks faster and more evenly. If using a conventional oven, increase the temperature by about 35°F (20°C) and rotate the pan halfway through baking.
Kala namak: also sold as black salt or Himalayan black salt. You can find it at Indian grocers or online. It gives the quiche an eggy taste. If you’re trying to lower sodium, sprinkle a pinch on the cooked slice instead of baking it, since it’s more pungent. 
Serving suggestion: This goes beautifully with a simple side of greens. Use any lettuce you like. I love arugula with this, dressed with a simple vinaigrette made with equal parts olive oil, Dijon mustard, and balsamic vinegar.
Leftovers: Let the quiche cool, then keep it covered in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Reheat slices in the oven or air fryer so the potato crust firms back up. It keeps in the fridge for 5 days; I do not recommend freezing.
Soy-free option: Replace the soy milk with unsweetened almond or oat milk. This will lower the protein count slightly, but be just as delicious.
